front: Explain the mechanism by which continuous (non-pulsatile) administration of Leuprolide leads to medical castration in prostate cancer management.
back: GnRH Receptor Downregulation. • Initial transient LH/FSH surge (flare). • Sustained dosing desensitizes pituitary gonadotropes. • Suppression of gonadotropin release leads to low testosterone.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Contrast the immediate physiological effects of GnRH antagonists like Degarelix with those of GnRH agonists like Leuprolide in oncology.
back: Prevention of Hormonal Flare. • Antagonists (Degarelix): Immediate suppression of LH/FSH. • Agonists (Leuprolide): Initial surge in testosterone. • Antagonists bypass the need for concurrent antiandrogens.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Identify the specific biochemical transformation inhibited by Finasteride in the treatment of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH).
back: Conversion of Testosterone to Dihydrotestosterone (DHT). • Inhibits 5-alpha reductase enzyme. • Reduces DHT, the potent androgen driving prostate growth. • Spares systemic testosterone levels.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Tamoxifen is termed a 'modulator' because it functions as an [___] in breast tissue but acts as an [___] in the endometrium and bone.
back: Antagonist; Agonist. • Breast: Competitively blocks estrogen receptors. • Endometrium: Agonist effect increases cancer risk. • Bone: Agonist effect prevents postmenopausal osteoporosis.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: A child with growth failure due to GH-receptor insensitivity (Laron syndrome) is treated with Mecasermin. This drug functions as a(n) [___].
back: Recombinant IGF-1 Agonist. • Bypasses defective or deficient GH receptors. • Directly activates IGF-1 receptors to promote growth. • Key side effect is hypoglycemia.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: How does Pegvisomant alter growth hormone signaling to treat acromegaly?
back: Growth Hormone Receptor Antagonism. • Mutant GH analog with two binding sites. • Allows receptor dimerization but prevents conformational change. • Blocks signal transduction and reduces IGF-1 levels.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Distinguish the primary contraceptive mechanism of Combined Oral Contraceptives (COCs) from that of Progestin-only 'mini-pills'.
back: Ovulation Inhibition vs Mucus Changes. • COCs: Suppress LH/FSH surge to prevent ovulation. • Progestin-only: Thicken cervical mucus to block sperm. • Progestin-only pills do not consistently inhibit ovulation.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Specify the role of Anastrozole in the hormonal therapy of postmenopausal breast cancer.
back: Aromatase Enzyme Inhibition. • Blocks conversion of androstenedione to estrone/estradiol. • Reduces peripheral estrogen production in postmenopausal women. • Ineffective in premenopausal women with active ovaries.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Somatropin promotes growth by acting through GH receptors to primarily increase the production of [___] in peripheral tissues.
back:
• Insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1).
• Mediates growth-promoting effects on bone and muscle.
• Also regulates lipid and carbohydrate metabolism and lean body mass.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: A 55-year-old male with advanced prostate cancer starts Leuprolide therapy. Explain why an androgen receptor antagonist like Flutamide is co-administered during the first week.
back:
• Prevents "tumor flare" caused by the initial surge in LH and testosterone.
• Continuous GnRH agonism eventually downregulates receptors.
• Antagonists block the effects of the transient hormonal rise.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Describe how Pegvisomant interferes with Growth Hormone signaling in patients with acromegaly.
back:
• Acts as a GH receptor antagonist.
• It is a mutant GH that binds one receptor but prevents dimerization.
• Blocks the conformational changes required for signal transduction.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Contrast the mechanism of pituitary suppression achieved by continuous Leuprolide administration versus Ganirelix.
back:
• Leuprolide (Agonist): Causes initial stimulation followed by receptor downregulation and desensitization.
• Ganirelix (Antagonist): Provides immediate, direct competitive blockade of GnRH receptors without an initial surge.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Specify the primary mechanism by which combined oral contraceptives (estrogen + progestin) prevent pregnancy.
back:
• Inhibition of ovulation via negative feedback.
• Suppresses pituitary release of FSH and LH.
• Secondary effects include thickening cervical mucus and altering endometrial receptivity.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: The clinical efficacy of Finasteride in treating benign prostatic hyperplasia depends on its ability to inhibit the enzyme [___].
back:
• 5α-reductase.
• Prevents conversion of testosterone to the more potent dihydrotestosterone (DHT).
• Reduces prostate size and male-pattern hair loss.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: A woman with a prolactinoma presents with galactorrhea and infertility. Explain the pharmacological basis for using Bromocriptine in her treatment.
back:
• Dopamine D2 receptor agonist.
• Mimics physiological dopamine to inhibit prolactin release from lactotrophs.
• Decreases serum prolactin, shrinks the tumor, and restores fertility.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Detail the mechanism of action of Mifepristone when used as an abortifacient.
back:
• Competitive antagonist at progesterone and glucocorticoid receptors.
• Causes decidual breakdown and luteolysis in early pregnancy.
• Sensitizes the uterus to the contractile effects of prostaglandins.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Distinguish the effect of Tamoxifen from Raloxifene on the endometrial lining.
back:
• Tamoxifen: Partial agonist on the endometrium; increases risk of hyperplasia/cancer.
• Raloxifene: Estrogen antagonist on the endometrium; lacks the risk of cancer induction.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Explain the receptor selectivity and primary renal mechanism of Desmopressin in treating Central Diabetes Insipidus.
back:
• Selective V2 receptor agonist.
• Triggers insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels into the apical membrane of collecting ducts.
• Increases water reabsorption and decreases urine volume.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Somatropin, the recombinant form of human GH, exerts its primary growth-promoting effects by stimulating the peripheral production of [___].
back:
* Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1)
* Produced primarily in the liver
* Mediates longitudinal bone growth and anabolic effects

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: A 45-year-old male with acromegaly is prescribed Octreotide. Describe the molecular mechanism by which this drug reduces growth hormone levels.
back:
* Somatostatin receptor agonist
* Inhibits GH release from anterior pituitary
* Suppresses additional hormones like glucagon and insulin

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Explain how continuous administration of Leuprolide leads to the suppression of the pituitary-gonadal axis.
back:
* GnRH receptor agonist
* Causes initial LH/FSH surge (flare)
* Subsequent downregulation and desensitization of pituitary GnRH receptors
* Resultant decrease in gonadal steroids

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: A patient with prostate cancer is started on Degarelix instead of Leuprolide to avoid 'tumor flare'. Contrast their mechanisms of action during the first week of therapy.
back:
* Degarelix: Pure GnRH antagonist; provides immediate suppression
* Leuprolide: GnRH agonist; causes transient testosterone surge (flare) before receptor downregulation

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Describe the specific enzymatic step targeted by Finasteride in the treatment of benign prostatic hyperplasia.
back:
* Inhibits 5-alpha-reductase
* Blocks conversion of Testosterone to Dihydrotestosterone (DHT)
* Reduces prostate size by limiting the more potent DHT stimulus

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Tamoxifen acts as an antagonist in breast tissue but behaves as an agonist in the [___], potentially increasing the risk of malignancy at that site.
back:
* Endometrium (Uterine tissue)
* Promotes endometrial hyperplasia
* Significant risk factor for endometrial cancer

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: A patient with a prolactinoma presents with galactorrhea. Explain the mechanism of the drug of choice, Bromocriptine, in this condition.
back:
* Dopamine D2 receptor agonist
* Mimics physiologic inhibitory effect of dopamine
* Directly suppresses prolactin secretion from pituitary lactotrophs

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Explain the molecular reason why Pegvisomant acts as a Growth Hormone antagonist despite binding to the same receptors as endogenous GH.
back:
* GH receptor antagonist
* Allows receptor dimerization but prevents conformational changes
* Blocks subsequent JAK/STAT signaling cascade

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Contrast the mechanism of action of Anastrozole and Fulvestrant in the treatment of hormone-responsive breast cancer.
back:
* Anastrozole: Nonsteroidal competitive aromatase inhibitor; blocks estrogen synthesis
* Fulvestrant: Pure estrogen receptor antagonist; causes receptor degradation

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Specify the receptor type and renal site of action for Desmopressin in the treatment of central diabetes insipidus.
back:
* V2 receptor agonist
* Acts on renal collecting ducts
* Increases aquaporin-2 insertion, promoting water reabsorption

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: The recombinant form of human growth hormone, Somatropin, exerts its primary growth-promoting effects by stimulating the production of [___] in peripheral tissues.
back:
• Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1).
• Produced primarily in the liver.
• Mediates longitudinal bone growth and anabolic metabolic effects.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: A 28-year-old female presents with galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and infertility. MRI reveals a prolactinoma. Identify the mechanism of action for the first-line pharmacological treatment.
back:
• Dopamine D2 receptor agonist.
• Inhibits prolactin release from the anterior pituitary lactotrophs.
• Examples include Bromocriptine and Cabergoline.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Describe how continuous administration of long-acting GnRH agonists (e.g., Leuprolide) leads to medical castration in prostate cancer patients.
back:
• Initial transient surge in LH and FSH (flare).
• Sustained use downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors.
• Causes pituitary desensitization and suppression of testosterone production.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Contrast the initial hormonal response of a GnRH receptor agonist versus a GnRH receptor antagonist in the treatment of advanced prostate cancer.
back:
• Agonists (Leuprolide): Cause an initial hormonal surge/flare.
• Antagonists (Degarelix): Immediate suppression of LH/FSH without a flare.
• Antagonists do not require antiandrogen co-administration.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Explain the specific biochemical step inhibited by Finasteride in the treatment of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH).
back:
• Inhibits the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase.
• Blocks conversion of Testosterone to Dihydrotestosterone (DHT).
• Reduces DHT levels to decrease prostatic volume.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Desmopressin treats central diabetes insipidus by acting as a selective agonist at [___] receptors in the renal collecting ducts.
back:
• Vasopressin V2 receptors.
• Increases water permeability via aquaporin-2 channel insertion.
• Lacks the V1-mediated vasoconstrictor effects of natural Vasopressin.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: A woman with PCOS seeking pregnancy is prescribed Clomiphene. Explain the mechanism by which this drug induces the LH surge required for ovulation.
back:
• Acts as a partial estrogen receptor agonist/antagonist.
• Blocks negative feedback of estrogen on the hypothalamus/pituitary.
• Triggers increased GnRH, FSH, and LH release.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Detail the dual receptor antagonism of Mifepristone when used as an abortifacient and its role in the luteolytic effect.
back:
• Competitive Progesterone receptor antagonist.
• Glucocorticoid receptor antagonist.
• Leads to decidual breakdown and increased uterine prostaglandin sensitivity.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Differentiate the effects of Tamoxifen and Raloxifene on endometrial tissue.
back:
• Tamoxifen: Estrogen agonist (increases risk of endometrial hyperplasia/cancer).
• Raloxifene: Estrogen antagonist (no increased endometrial cancer risk).
• Both are bone agonists and breast antagonists.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Define the mechanism of action for Anastrozole in the management of postmenopausal breast cancer.
back:
• Nonsteroidal competitive inhibitor of Aromatase.
• Blocks the conversion of androstenedione to estrone/estradiol.
• Reduces circulating estrogen levels in peripheral tissues.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Somatropin exerts its primary growth-promoting effects by stimulating the production of [___] in the liver and peripheral tissues.
back:
• IGF-1 (Insulin-like growth factor-1)
• Mediates metabolic and growth effects of GH
• Deficiency in IGF-1 requires treatment with Mecasermin.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: A 50-year-old male with acromegaly is prescribed Octreotide. Explain the mechanism by which this drug reduces GH levels.
back:
• Acts as a somatostatin receptor agonist
• Mimics endogenous somatostatin to inhibit GH release from pituitary
• Also inhibits insulin, glucagon, and gastrin.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Describe the physiological process by which continuous (non-pulsatile) administration of Leuprolide suppresses the gonadal axis.
back:
• Causes downregulation of pituitary GnRH receptors
• Leads to pituitary desensitization
• Results in suppression of LH and FSH secretion.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Contrast the pharmacological targets of Finasteride versus Flutamide in the management of prostatic disease.
back:
• Finasteride: Inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, preventing conversion of Testosterone to DHT
• Flutamide: Competitive antagonist at androgen receptors
• Finasteride preserves testosterone-mediated libido better.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Outline the mechanism of action for Clomiphene in the treatment of female infertility.
back:
• Partial agonist/antagonist at estrogen receptors in pituitary
• Blocks negative feedback of endogenous estrogen
• Increases pulsatile GnRH, FSH, and LH release to trigger ovulation.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Mifepristone functions as a competitive antagonist at both the [___] and glucocorticoid receptors, commonly used for medical abortion.
back:
• Progesterone receptor
• Leads to decidual breakdown and sensitizes the uterus to prostaglandins.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: A female on combined oral contraceptives (COCs) is treated with Rifampin for TB. Why is there a high risk of contraceptive failure?
back:
• Rifampin is a potent CYP3A4 inducer
• Accelerates hepatic metabolism of estrogen and progestins
• Reduces serum levels below the therapeutic threshold for ovulation suppression.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: How does the clinical mechanism of Ganirelix differ from Leuprolide during the initiation phase of IVF protocols?
back:
• Ganirelix (Antagonist): Immediate suppression of gonadotropins; no flare
• Leuprolide (Agonist): Initial FSH/LH surge (flare) before receptor downregulation occurs.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Distinguish between the endometrial effects of Tamoxifen and Raloxifene.
back:
• Tamoxifen: Estrogen agonist on endometrium (risk of hyperplasia/cancer)
• Raloxifene: Estrogen antagonist on endometrium (no cancer risk)
• Both are bone agonists.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Describe the mechanism by which Desmopressin reduces polyuria in central diabetes insipidus.
back:
• Selective agonist for V2 receptors
• Increases insertion of aquaporin-2 water channels in renal collecting ducts
• Enhances free water reabsorption.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Somatropin, the recombinant form of human GH, promotes linear growth primarily by stimulating the hepatic production of [___].
back:
• Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1)
• IGF-1 acts on peripheral tissues (bone/muscle) to mediate growth
• Somatropin binds to specific GH receptors (JAK/STAT pathway)

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: A patient with acromegaly is prescribed Pegvisomant. Describe the specific molecular interaction this drug has with its target receptor.
back:
• Growth hormone (GH) receptor antagonist
• Binds to GH receptors but prevents necessary dimerization
• Blocks conformational changes required for signal transduction

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Explain the cellular mechanism of action for Bromocriptine in treating a prolactinoma.
back:
• Dopamine D2 receptor agonist
• Mimics physiological dopamine inhibition at the pituitary
• Directly suppresses prolactin secretion from lactotrophs

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: In a patient starting Leuprolide for prostate cancer, explain why Flutamide is often co-administered during the first week of therapy.
back:
• Leuprolide causes an initial 'flare' (agonist effect)
• Flutamide blocks androgen receptors to prevent tumor stimulation
• Prevents worsening of symptoms during the transition to receptor downregulation

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Summarize the pharmacological step inhibited by Finasteride in the treatment of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH).
back:
• Inhibits 5-alpha reductase enzyme
• Blocks conversion of Testosterone to Dihydrotestosterone (DHT)
• Reduces prostate volume without lowering systemic testosterone levels

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Tamoxifen acts as a competitive [___] in breast tissue and an [___] in the endometrium and bone.
back:
• Estrogen receptor (ER) antagonist (breast)
• Estrogen receptor (ER) agonist (bone/uterus)
• Classification: Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM)

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: A 28-year-old female is prescribed Mifepristone for medical abortion. Explain its primary mechanism on the uterine lining.
back:
• Competitive Progesterone receptor antagonist
• Causes decidual breakdown and blastocyst detachment
• Often combined with Misoprostol (prostaglandin) to induce contractions

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Contrast the mechanism of Ganirelix with continuous Leuprolide administration in the context of ovulation induction.
back:
• Ganirelix: Competitive GnRH antagonist; immediate suppression of LH/FSH
• Leuprolide: GnRH agonist; causes downregulation/internalization of receptors
• Ganirelix avoids the 'flare' effect seen with agonists

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Distinguish between the enzymatic targets of Anastrozole and Exemestane.
back:
• Anastrozole: Reversible, nonsteroidal competitive aromatase inhibitor
• Exemestane: Irreversible, steroidal aromatase inactivator
• Both block the conversion of androstenedione to estrone/estradiol

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Identify the receptor and intracellular signaling pathway activated by Desmopressin in the renal collecting duct.
back:
• Vasopressin V2 receptors
• Activates Gs-protein/Adenylate Cyclase pathway
• Increases cAMP, leading to aquaporin-2 insertion in apical membranes

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Steady dosing with the long-acting GnRH agonist Leuprolide inhibits gonadotropin release by [___] GnRH receptors in the anterior pituitary.
back:
Downregulating
- Continuous (non-pulsatile) administration causes receptor internalization.
- Results in profound suppression of LH and FSH secretion.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: A 45-year-old male with acromegaly is treated with Pegvisomant. This drug controls the disease by [___].
back:
Blocking Growth Hormone (GH) receptor signaling
- Prevents GH-induced receptor dimerization.
- Unlike somatostatin analogs, it does not inhibit GH secretion.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Explain the molecular mechanism of action of Clomiphene in the treatment of female infertility.
back:
Pituitary Estrogen Receptor Blockade
- Acts as a partial agonist/antagonist.
- Blocks negative feedback of estrogen at the pituitary.
- Increases pulsatile GnRH, FSH, and LH release to induce ovulation.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: A postmenopausal woman with a high risk of breast cancer and a history of endometrial polyps requires osteoporosis prophylaxis. Contrast why Raloxifene is preferred over Tamoxifen in this patient.
back:
Endometrial Tissue Specificity
- Raloxifene: Estrogen antagonist in the uterus (no cancer risk).
- Tamoxifen: Estrogen agonist in the uterus (increases risk of hyperplasia/cancer).
- Both are agonists in bone.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: State the specific biochemical step inhibited by Finasteride in the management of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH).
back:
Inhibition of 5-alpha-Reductase
- Blocks the conversion of Testosterone to Dihydrotestosterone (DHT).
- Reduces the primary androgen stimulant for prostatic growth.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: In patients with a prolactinoma, Bromocriptine restores fertility by acting as an agonist at [___] receptors to inhibit prolactin release.
back:
Dopamine D2 Receptors
- Mimics the physiologic inhibitory effect of dopamine on lactotrophs.
- Decreases prolactin levels, allowing normal GnRH pulsatility to resume.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Somatropin, the recombinant human growth hormone, exerts its primary growth-promoting effects by stimulating the peripheral production of [___] in the liver.
back:
• Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1).
• Mediates anabolic effects on bone and muscle.
• Somatropin acts via JAK/STAT receptors.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: A 28-year-old female presents with galactorrhea and infertility due to a prolactinoma. The drug prescribed to restore her fertility works by [___].
back:
• Activating Dopamine D2 receptors.
• Directly inhibits prolactin release from the anterior pituitary.
• Examples include Bromocriptine and Cabergoline.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Explain the molecular mechanism by which continuous administration of Leuprolide leads to medical castration in prostate cancer patients.
back:
• Initial transient stimulation of GnRH receptors causes an LH/FSH surge.
• Prolonged exposure leads to downregulation/desensitization of pituitary GnRH receptors.
• Resulting suppression of gonadotropins reduces testosterone to castrate levels.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Contrast the onset of action between GnRH antagonists (e.g., Ganirelix) and GnRH agonists (e.g., Leuprolide) when used to suppress LH surges.
back:
• GnRH Antagonists: Provide immediate suppression of LH/FSH without an initial flare.
• GnRH Agonists: Require roughly one week of continuous dosing to achieve suppression via receptor downregulation.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Identify the specific enzymatic conversion inhibited by Finasteride in the treatment of androgenic alopecia and BPH.
back:
• Inhibits 5-alpha reductase.
• Prevents conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT).
• DHT is the primary androgen responsible for prostate growth and hair follicle miniaturization.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Tamoxifen, a Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulator (SERM), acts as an [___] in breast tissue but as an [___] in the endometrium.
back:
• Antagonist (breast tissue).
• Agonist (endometrium and bone).
• Increases risk of endometrial hyperplasia/cancer while treating breast cancer.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: A postmenopausal woman with ER-positive breast cancer is started on Anastrozole. Describe the biochemical pathway this drug targets.
back:
• Inhibits Aromatase (CYP19).
• Blocks the final step of estrogen synthesis (conversion of androstenedione/testosterone to estrogens).
• Primary source of estrogen in postmenopausal women is peripheral aromatization.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: In the context of medical abortion, compare the mechanisms of Mifepristone and Misoprostol.
back:
• Mifepristone: Competitive progesterone receptor antagonist; causes decidual breakdown.
• Misoprostol: PGE1 analog; induces uterine contractions and cervical ripening.

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Distinguish the renal mechanism of Desmopressin from the vascular effect of high-dose Vasopressin.
back:
• Desmopressin: Selective V2 receptor agonist; increases aquaporin-2 channels in collecting ducts (antidiuresis).
• Vasopressin: V1 receptor agonist; causes contraction of vascular smooth muscle (vasoconstriction).

category: Explain their mechanism of action
front: Describe the cellular mechanism by which Oxytocin facilitates the 'let-down' reflex and labor induction.
back:
• Binds G protein-coupled oxytocin receptors.
• Increases intracellular calcium levels.
• Stimulates contraction of myoepithelial cells (milk let-down) and uterine smooth muscle (labor).

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Somatropin exerts its primary growth-promoting and metabolic effects by stimulating the peripheral production of [___].
back:
• Insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1).
• Produced mainly in the liver.
• Mediates longitudinal bone growth and protein synthesis.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 45-year-old male with acromegaly is treated with Octreotide. He subsequently develops right upper quadrant pain after meals. Identify the most likely pharmacological cause.
back:
• Biliary sludge or Gallstones.
• Octreotide inhibits postprandial gallbladder contractility.
• It also reduces pancreatic enzyme secretion and cholecystokinin release.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Describe the physiological mechanism by which Bromocriptine treats the amenorrhea-galactorrhea syndrome.
back:
• D2 Receptor Agonism: Acts as a dopamine substitute in the pituitary.
• Prolactin Inhibition: Directly suppresses prolactin secretion from lactotrophs.
• GnRH Restoration: Lower prolactin levels allow normal pulsatile GnRH release and ovulation.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A woman with breast cancer is switched from Tamoxifen to Fulvestrant due to resistance. Contrast the estrogen receptor dynamics between these two agents.
back:
• Tamoxifen: A SERM; acts as an antagonist in breast but an agonist in bone and endometrium.
• Fulvestrant: A pure antagonist; induces global estrogen receptor degradation (downregulation) in all tissues.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Explain the paradoxical development of gynecomastia and testicular atrophy in men using high doses of anabolic steroids.
back:
• Aromatization: Excess exogenous testosterone is converted to estrogen by peripheral aromatase.
• Negative Feedback: High levels inhibit the HPG axis, suppressing endogenous LH/FSH and testosterone production.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: The enzyme responsible for converting testosterone to the more potent androgen dihydrotestosterone (DHT) in the prostate is inhibited by [___].
back:
• 5-alpha-reductase.
• Inhibited by Finasteride or Dutasteride.
• Used to treat BPH and male-pattern baldness.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 22-year-old female requires emergency contraception 48 hours post-unprotected intercourse. Which steroid antagonist provides both postcoital contraception and abortifacient properties?
back:
• Mifepristone (RU-486).
• Mechanism: Competitive progesterone and glucocorticoid receptor antagonist.
• Effect: Causes decidual breakdown and sensitizes the uterus to prostaglandins.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Discuss the clinical reasoning for administering Flutamide during the first week of Leuprolide therapy in advanced prostate cancer.
back:
• Prevention of 'Tumor Flare'.
• Leuprolide initially acts as a GnRH agonist, causing a transient surge in testosterone.
• Flutamide blocks androgen receptors, preventing stimulation of cancer cells during this surge.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Contrast the clinical indications of Desmopressin and Vasopressin based on their receptor selectivity.
back:
• Desmopressin: V2-selective; used for Central Diabetes Insipidus and Von Willebrand Disease.
• Vasopressin: Non-selective (V1 & V2); used for esophageal variceal bleeding due to V1-mediated vasoconstriction.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Identify the primary mechanism of action and the major cardiovascular risk associated with the estrogen component of Combined Oral Contraceptives.
back:
• Action: Inhibits ovulation by suppressing mid-cycle LH surge via negative feedback.
• Adverse Effect: Thromboembolism (DVT/PE) due to increased hepatic synthesis of clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X).

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: In children with Turner syndrome or chronic renal failure, the recombinant human growth hormone used to increase final adult height is [___].
back:
- Somatropin.
- Clinical uses: GH deficiency, AIDS wasting, short bowel syndrome.
- Adverse effects: Pseudotumor cerebri, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, hyperglycemia, and peripheral edema.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 45-year-old male with acromegaly fails surgical resection of a pituitary tumor. Identify the first-line somatostatin analog and its common biliary complication.
back:
- Octreotide (or Lanreotide).
- Clinical use: Acromegaly, carcinoid syndrome, and esophageal variceal bleeding.
- Adverse effects: Biliary sludge/gallstones (inhibits cholecystokinin), steatorrhea, and bradycardia.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Explain the mechanism by which continuous (non-pulsatile) administration of Leuprolide treats advanced prostate cancer.
back:
- Mechanism: Downregulates pituitary GnRH receptors.
- Result: Inhibits LH and FSH release, leading to castrate levels of testosterone.
- Adverse effects: Hot flushes, osteoporosis, and initial 'tumor flare'.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman requires treatment for osteoporosis but has a high risk of breast cancer. Contrast the endometrial effects of Tamoxifen versus Raloxifene.
back:
- Tamoxifen: Agonist at endometrium (increases cancer risk).
- Raloxifene: Antagonist at endometrium (no cancer risk).
- Both: Antagonists in breast (prevent cancer) and agonists in bone.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Identify the clinical uses of Desmopressin (DDAVP) and its most critical electrolyte-related adverse effect.
back:
- Uses: Central diabetes insipidus, Hemophilia A, and von Willebrand disease.
- Mechanism: Selective V2 receptor agonist.
- Adverse effect: Dilutional hyponatremia (water intoxication).

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: To prevent the 'tumor flare' phenomenon caused by the initial testosterone surge during GnRH agonist therapy, the drug [___] is co-administered.
back:
- Flutamide (or Bicalutamide).
- Class: Competitive androgen receptor antagonist.
- Clinical use: Advanced prostate cancer.
- Adverse effects: Gynecomastia, hot flushes, and hepatotoxicity.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A woman on combined oral contraceptives (COCs) starts Rifampin for tuberculosis. Predict the effect on her contraceptive therapy and the underlying mechanism.
back:
- Outcome: Reduced contraceptive efficacy/unintended pregnancy.
- Mechanism: Rifampin induces Cytochrome P450 (CYP3A4) enzymes.
- Result: Increased hepatic metabolism of ethinyl estradiol and progestin.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Explain the role of Bromocriptine in treating a patient with a prolactinoma presenting with galactorrhea and infertility.
back:
- Mechanism: Dopamine D2 receptor agonist.
- Function: Mimics endogenous dopamine to inhibit prolactin release from the anterior pituitary.
- Adverse effects: Nausea, orthostatic hypotension, and psychiatric disturbances.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Contrast the enzyme targeted by Finasteride with the receptor targeted by Spironolactone in the treatment of hirsutism.
back:
- Finasteride: Inhibits 5-alpha reductase (blocks DHT synthesis).
- Spironolactone: Competitively antagonizes androgen receptors (blocks binding).
- Finasteride Use: BPH and male-pattern baldness.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Enumerate the primary clinical use and the major metabolic toxicity of Mecasermin.
back:
- Use: Growth failure in children with severe IGF-1 deficiency (Laron dwarfism).
- Toxicity: Hypoglycemia (due to insulin-like growth factor activity).
- Other effect: Intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri).

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Somatropin, the recombinant form of human Growth Hormone, is primarily used for the treatment of [___] in children and AIDS-associated wasting in adults.
back:
• Growth hormone deficiency
• Turner syndrome
• Prader-Willi syndrome
• Chronic renal failure

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 50-year-old male with acromegaly is prescribed a somatostatin analog. Identify the drug and its most significant gastrointestinal side effect related to the gallbladder.
back:
• Drug: Octreotide (or Lanreotide)
• Adverse effect: Cholelithiasis (gallstones) due to inhibition of cholecystokinin release and gallbladder contractility.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Explain the pharmacodynamic mechanism by which continuous (non-pulsatile) administration of Leuprolide manages advanced prostate cancer.
back:
• Initial 'flare' of LH/FSH secretion
• Downregulation of GnRH receptors in the pituitary
• Eventual suppression of gonadotropins
• Reduction of testosterone to castrate levels

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Contrast the initial effect on gonadotropin levels between GnRH agonists (e.g., Leuprolide) and GnRH antagonists (e.g., Ganirelix) in the first 48 hours of therapy.
back:
• Leuprolide: Transient increase (surge) in LH and FSH ('flare' effect).
• Ganirelix: Immediate suppression of LH and FSH without an initial surge.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: List the clinical applications and major cardiovascular/neurological side effects of Bromocriptine.
back:
• Uses: Prolactinomas, acromegaly, Parkinson's disease
• Side Effects: Orthostatic hypotension, nausea, psychiatric disturbances (hallucinations), and digital vasospasm.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: The synthetic analog of vasopressin used for central diabetes insipidus and nocturnal enuresis, which acts selectively on V2 receptors, is [___].
back:
• Desmopressin (dDAVP)
• Also used in mild Hemophilia A and von Willebrand disease to increase Factor VIII levels.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 55-year-old female smoker on HRT (Estrogen + Progestin) is at significant risk for which specific life-threatening vascular complication?
back:
• Thromboembolism (DVT, Pulmonary Embolism)
• Myocardial infarction
• Stroke
• Risk is exacerbated by smoking and age.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Describe the mechanism of action of Clomiphene in treating female infertility.
back:
• Partial estrogen receptor agonist
• Blocks estrogen's negative feedback on the pituitary/hypothalamus
• Increases pulsatile GnRH, FSH, and LH release
• Stimulates follicle development and ovulation.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Distinguish between the mechanisms of Finasteride and Flutamide in the management of prostate disease.
back:
• Finasteride: 5-alpha reductase inhibitor; prevents conversion of Testosterone to Dihydrotestosterone (DHT).
• Flutamide: Competitive antagonist at the androgen receptor.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Identify the primary clinical use of Mifepristone and its mechanism during early pregnancy.
back:
• Use: Medical abortifacient (with misoprostol)
• Mechanism: Progesterone receptor antagonist; causes breakdown of the decidua and sensitization of the uterus to prostaglandins.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A specific adverse effect of Somatropin therapy in children, characterized by increased intracranial pressure without a tumor, is [___].
back:
- Pseudotumor cerebri (idiopathic intracranial hypertension).
- Requires monitoring of fundoscopy for papilledema.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 50-year-old male with acromegaly on long-term Octreotide therapy develops right upper quadrant pain. This clinical finding is most likely due to the drug's effect on [___].
back:
- Inhibition of gallbladder contractility.
- Leads to biliary sludge and gallstone formation (cholelithiasis).

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Explain the mechanism by which Clomiphene induces ovulation in women with anovulatory infertility.
back:
- Acts as a partial estrogen agonist in the pituitary.
- Blocks negative feedback, increasing FSH and LH secretion to stimulate follicular maturation.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Contrast the initial hormonal response of GnRH agonists (e.g., Leuprolide) with GnRH antagonists (e.g., Degarelix) in the treatment of advanced prostate cancer.
back:
- Agonists: Cause transient 'tumor flare' due to initial testosterone surge.
- Antagonists: Provide immediate testosterone suppression without an initial surge/flare.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Enumerate the primary clinical uses of Desmopressin (V2-selective agonist) other than Central Diabetes Insipidus.
back:
- Mild Hemophilia A (increases Factor VIII).
- Von Willebrand Disease (increases vWF).
- Primary nocturnal enuresis.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: The primary enzyme inhibited by Finasteride to prevent male-pattern baldness and treat benign prostatic hyperplasia is [___].
back:
- 5-alpha-reductase.
- Reduces conversion of Testosterone to the more potent Dihydrotestosterone (DHT).

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 55-year-old female on Tamoxifen for breast cancer treatment presents with abnormal vaginal bleeding. This finding necessitates evaluation for [___].
back:
- Endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma.
- Caused by Tamoxifen's agonist effect on uterine estrogen receptors.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Explain the mechanism behind the most common acute adverse effect of Mecasermin (Recombinant IGF-1).
back:
- IGF-1 possesses insulin-like activity.
- Directly stimulates glucose uptake, leading to significant hypoglycemia.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Contrast the clinical use of Oxytocin with the potential use of Atosiban in obstetric practice.
back:
- Oxytocin: Receptor agonist used to induce or augment labor.
- Atosiban: Receptor antagonist used as a tocolytic to suppress preterm labor.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Identify the major vascular adverse effect of estrogen-containing oral contraceptives that is exacerbated by smoking.
back:
- Thromboembolic events.
- Includes Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT), Pulmonary Embolism, and Stroke.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: The recombinant form of human growth hormone (GH) used for replacement therapy in children with Turner Syndrome and Prader-Willi Syndrome is [___].
back:
Somatropin
- Acts through GH receptors to increase IGF-1
- Adverse effects: Pseudotumor cerebri, hyperglycemia, and edema

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 45-year-old male with acromegaly being treated with Octreotide presents with right upper quadrant pain. This clinical finding is a known side effect caused by [___].
back:
Gallstones (biliary sludge)
- Octreotide inhibits gallbladder contractility
- Other AEs: GI disturbances (steatorrhea), bradycardia, and conduction anomalies

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Explain the cellular mechanism through which continuous administration of GnRH agonists like Leuprolide suppresses the production of FSH and LH.
back:
- Initial surge: Transient LH/FSH release
- Downregulation: Desensitization of GnRH receptors in the anterior pituitary
- Net result: Suppression of gonadal steroidogenesis

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Contrast the clinical use of GnRH agonists (e.g., Leuprolide) versus GnRH antagonists (e.g., Degarelix) in the management of advanced prostate cancer.
back:
- Agonists: Require anti-androgen (Flutamide) to prevent 'tumor flare' surge
- Antagonists: Cause immediate testosterone drop without initial surge
- Both lead to chemical castration

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Identify the primary clinical uses of Tamoxifen and its most serious dose-dependent adverse effect regarding the uterus.
back:
- Uses: ER-positive breast cancer (treatment and prophylaxis)
- Adverse Effect: Increased risk of endometrial hyperplasia and cancer (agonist effect in uterus)

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: The selective V2 receptor agonist used as the first-line treatment for central diabetes insipidus and mild Hemophilia A is [___].
back:
Desmopressin (DDAVP)
- Increases water reabsorption in renal collecting ducts
- Releases von Willebrand factor and Factor VIII

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 28-year-old female undergoing ovulation induction with Menotropins presents with sudden-onset ascites, hypovolemia, and pleural effusion. Identify this condition.
back:
Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS)
- Caused by excessive follicle stimulation
- Complication of FSH/LH or hCG therapy

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Explain why Mecasermin is used in certain children with growth failure and identify its most critical acute metabolic complication.
back:
- Use: GH-insensitivity syndrome (Laron dwarfism) where GH receptors are non-functional
- AE: Hypoglycemia (IGF-1 has insulin-like effects; must eat before dosing)

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Distinguish the pharmacological targets of Finasteride and Flutamide in the treatment of prostate-related pathologies.
back:
- Finasteride: Inhibits 5-alpha-reductase (blocks conversion of testosterone to DHT)
- Flutamide: Competitive antagonist at androgen receptors

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: List two therapeutic uses for Bromocriptine and its primary mechanism of action.
back:
- Mechanism: Dopamine D2 receptor agonist
- Uses: Hyperprolactinemia (prolactinoma) and Parkinson's disease

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A rare but serious adverse effect of [___] therapy in children is pseudotumor cerebri, often presenting with headache and papilledema.
back:
• Somatropin (Recombinant Growth Hormone)
• Used for GH deficiency and Turner syndrome
• Monitoring for hyperglycemia and slipped capital femoral epiphysis is also required.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 45-year-old male with acromegaly and a large pituitary adenoma is prescribed a somatostatin analog. Name the most common biliary complication associated with this drug.
back:
• Gallstones (Cholelithiasis)
• Caused by Octreotide/Lanreotide
• Mechanism: Inhibition of gallbladder contractility and reduction of bile flow.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Explain how clomiphene induces ovulation in anovulatory women seeking pregnancy.
back:
• Acts as a partial estrogen agonist
• Blocks estrogen receptors in the pituitary
• Reduces negative feedback, leading to increased pulsatile GnRH, FSH, and LH release.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Contrast the initial hormonal response of Leuprolide versus Degarelix in the treatment of advanced prostate cancer.
back:
• Leuprolide (Agonist): Causes transient 'tumor flare' due to initial testosterone surge.
• Degarelix (Antagonist): Provides immediate testosterone suppression without an initial surge.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Identify the specific enzymatic step inhibited by Finasteride in the treatment of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH).
back:
• Inhibits 5-alpha-reductase
• Blocks the conversion of Testosterone to Dihydrotestosterone (DHT)
• Specifically targets DHT-dependent tissues like the prostate and hair follicles.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: The primary pharmacological treatment for hyperprolactinemia-induced infertility and galactorrhea is [___], which acts as a D2 receptor agonist.
back:
• Bromocriptine (or Cabergoline)
• Mechanism: Mimics dopamine to inhibit prolactin release from the anterior pituitary
• Restores ovulation and fertility.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A postmenopausal woman with a high risk of breast cancer and osteoporosis is started on Raloxifene. Why is this preferred over Tamoxifen regarding endometrial safety?
back:
• Raloxifene is an estrogen antagonist in the uterus
• Tamoxifen acts as a partial agonist in the endometrium
• Tamoxifen increases risk of endometrial hyperplasia/cancer; Raloxifene does not.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Detail why Desmopressin (dDAVP) is preferred over natural Vasopressin for treating Central Diabetes Insipidus.
back:
• High selectivity for V2 receptors over V1 receptors
• Lacks significant vasoconstrictor effects (V1-mediated)
• Possesses a longer half-life and better oral/nasal bioavailability.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Distinguish the metabolic risk of Oral Contraceptives in a 40-year-old smoker compared to a non-smoker.
back:
• Significantly higher risk of Thromboembolism (MI, stroke, DVT)
• Estrogen increases hepatic synthesis of clotting factors
• Smoking synergistically enhances vascular damage and hypercoagulability.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Specify the hormone receptor targeted by Mifepristone when used as an abortifacient.
back:
• Progesterone receptor antagonist
• Also blocks Glucocorticoid receptors
• Often used with Misoprostol (PGE1 analog) to induce medical abortion.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: The recombinant form of human growth hormone, [___], is used for GH deficiency but may cause serious adverse effects in children such as pseudotumor cerebri and slipped capital femoral epiphysis.
back:
• Somatropin
• Promotes IGF-1 production
• Other toxicities: Edema, hyperglycemia, and progression of scoliosis

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 45-year-old male with coarsened facial features and enlarged hands fails surgery for a pituitary adenoma. Identify the long-acting somatostatin analog used to inhibit GH secretion in this patient.
back:
• Octreotide (or Lanreotide)
• Mechanism: Somatostatin receptor agonist
• Clinical Use: Acromegaly, carcinoid syndrome, and gastrinoma

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Explain the biphasic mechanism of continuous Leuprolide administration in the treatment of advanced prostate cancer.
back:
• Initial Phase: Transient surge (flare) of LH and FSH
• Chronic Phase: Downregulation of GnRH receptors
• Result: Suppression of gonadotropin and testosterone secretion

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Contrast the effects of Tamoxifen and Raloxifene on the endometrial lining and their clinical significance.
back:
• Tamoxifen: Agonist (increases risk of endometrial hyperplasia/cancer)
• Raloxifene: Antagonist (no risk of endometrial cancer)
• Both act as antagonists in breast tissue

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: List the paradoxical adverse effects of high-dose anabolic steroids on the male reproductive system.
back:
• Feminization (Gynecomastia)
• Testicular shrinkage
• Infertility
• Mechanism: Feedback inhibition of pituitary and conversion to estrogens

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: The selective V2 receptor agonist [___] is the treatment of choice for central diabetes insipidus and mild Hemophilia A.
back:
• Desmopressin (DDAVP)
• Mechanism: Increases water reabsorption and release of Factor VIII/von Willebrand factor
• Toxicity: Hyponatremia and headache

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 28-year-old female presents with galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and infertility. State the drug class and primary side effects used to restore her fertility.
back:
• Dopamine D2 Receptor Agonists (e.g., Bromocriptine)
• Adverse effects: Nausea, headache, and orthostatic hypotension
• Psychiatric disturbances can occur at high doses

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Describe how Finasteride treats benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) without significantly reducing libido compared to other antiandrogens.
back:
• Mechanism: Inhibits 5-alpha reductase (Type II)
• Prevents conversion of Testosterone to Dihydrotestosterone (DHT) in prostate
• Spares systemic testosterone levels

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Distinguish between GnRH agonists (e.g., Leuprolide) and GnRH antagonists (e.g., Ganirelix) regarding their immediate effect on gonadotropin secretion.
back:
• Agonists: Initial stimulation of LH/FSH (Tumor Flare)
• Antagonists: Immediate suppression without initial surge
• Antagonists are preferred to avoid tumor flare in prostate cancer

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Identify the clinical use and the most common complication of the Mifepristone-Misoprostol drug combination.
back:
• Clinical Use: Medical abortifacient (up to 49 days gestation)
• Complication: Failure to induce complete abortion
• Adverse effects: Vaginal bleeding, cramping, and GI distress

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: The recombinant form of human growth hormone used to treat children with Turner syndrome or Prader-Willi syndrome is [___].
back:
Somatropin. 
• Mechanism: Stimulates IGF-1 production in the liver.
• Key Use: Growth hormone deficiency, HIV wasting, and short bowel syndrome.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 7-year-old post-chemotherapy patient presents with excessive thirst, polyuria, and hypernatremia. Which specific V2 receptor agonist is indicated for this condition?
back:
Desmopressin (dDAVP). 
• Diagnosis: Pituitary (central) diabetes insipidus.
• Mechanism: Increases water permeability in renal collecting ducts.
• Adverse Effect: Hyponatremia.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which continuous (non-pulsatile) administration of Leuprolide suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.
back:
GnRH Receptor Downregulation. 
• Initial Effect: Transient surge (flare) of LH and FSH.
• Chronic Effect: Downregulation of pituitary GnRH receptors, leading to decreased gonadal steroids.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Contrast the pharmacological effects of Tamoxifen and Raloxifene on the endometrial lining in postmenopausal women.
back:
Tamoxifen: Estrogen agonist (increases risk of endometrial hyperplasia/cancer).
• Raloxifene: Estrogen antagonist (no increased risk of endometrial cancer).

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Identify the primary clinical uses and two hallmark metabolic adverse effects of the somatostatin analog Octreotide.
back:
Uses: Acromegaly, carcinoid syndrome, and esophageal varices.
• Adverse Effects: Biliary sludge/gallstones (inhibition of cholecystokinin) and steatorrhea (nausea/cramps).

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: The steroid antagonist used in combination with Misoprostol to achieve medical abortion up to 49 days of gestation is [___].
back:
Mifepristone (RU 486). 
• Mechanism: Competitively blocks progesterone and glucocorticoid receptors.
• Adverse Effect: Significant vaginal bleeding and GI distress.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 60-year-old male with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is prescribed Finasteride. How does this drug reduce prostate size without causing infertility?
back:
5-alpha Reductase Inhibition. 
• Action: Blocks conversion of Testosterone to Dihydrotestosterone (DHT).
• Logic: DHT is the primary androgen in the prostate; Testosterone levels remain maintained for libido.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Evaluate why GnRH receptor antagonists (e.g., Degarelix) are preferred over agonists (e.g., Leuprolide) in the immediate management of advanced prostate cancer with bone metastases.
back:
Prevention of 'Tumor Flare'. 
• Antagonists cause immediate drop in testosterone without the initial agonist-induced testosterone surge that worsens bone pain or spinal cord compression.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Distinguish between the primary clinical indications for Clomiphene and Bromocriptine in the management of female infertility.
back:
Clomiphene: Used for anovulation (blocks estrogen feedback to increase FSH/LH).
• Bromocriptine: Used for hyperprolactinemia (D2 agonist that inhibits prolactin release).

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: List the most common dose-dependent adverse effects associated with Combined Oral Contraceptives (COCs).
back:
Thromboembolism (DVT/PE).
• Hypertension.
• Breakthrough bleeding.
• Nausea, breast tenderness, and migraine exacerbation.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Somatropin, the recombinant form of human GH, mediates its effects primarily by regulating the production of [___] in peripheral tissues like the liver.
back: Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1). It is used for growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, and AIDS-associated wasting.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A child receiving Somatropin for short stature suddenly develops severe headaches and papilledema. Identify the most likely underlying adverse effect.
back: Pseudotumor cerebri (idiopathic intracranial hypertension). Other serious side effects include slipped capital femoral epiphysis and hyperglycemia.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Explain the mechanism by which continuous, non-pulsatile administration of Leuprolide leads to the suppression of gonadal steroids.
back: It downregulates GnRH receptors in the pituitary. This inhibits the release of LH and FSH, leading to decreased estrogen or testosterone production.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Contrast the clinical presentation of the 'tumor flare' phenomenon when using Leuprolide versus Ganirelix in the treatment of advanced prostate cancer.
back: Leuprolide (agonist) causes an initial testosterone surge/flare before suppression. Ganirelix (antagonist) provides immediate suppression without any surge or tumor flare.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Name the primary clinical uses of Bromocriptine and identify the psychiatric contraindication for its use.
back: Uses: Hyperprolactinemia (prolactinoma), Parkinson's disease, and Acromegaly. Contraindication: History of psychosis or schizophrenia due to D2 receptor stimulation.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: In patients with mild Hemophilia A or von Willebrand disease, [___] is administered to increase plasma levels of Factor VIII and vWF.
back: Desmopressin (DDAVP). It acts on extrarenal V2 receptors to trigger the release of these clotting factors from storage sites.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 22-year-old female presents with clear cell vaginal adenocarcinoma and a history of maternal drug exposure during pregnancy. Identify the causative agent.
back: Diethylstilbestrol (DES). It is associated with vaginal adenocarcinoma, infertility, and uterine abnormalities in the daughters of treated women.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A postmenopausal woman requires treatment for osteoporosis but has a high risk of endometrial cancer. Compare the suitability of Tamoxifen versus Raloxifene for this patient.
back: Raloxifene is preferred. Unlike Tamoxifen, Raloxifene is an antagonist in the endometrium and does not increase the risk of endometrial cancer.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Distinguish between the enzyme-level mechanism of Finasteride and the receptor-level mechanism of Flutamide in managing prostate conditions.
back: Finasteride: Inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, blocking conversion of Testosterone to DHT. Flutamide: Competitive antagonist at the androgen receptor itself.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: What is the most common acute adverse effect of Mecasermin (recombinant IGF-1) and how is it clinically managed?
back: Hypoglycemia. It is managed by advising the patient to consume a carbohydrate-containing snack or meal shortly before the injection.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: The recombinant human growth hormone used for growth failure in Turner syndrome and chronic renal failure is [___].
back:
Somatropin
*   **Clinical Uses:** GH deficiency, Prader-Willi syndrome, AIDS wasting.
*   **Adverse Effects:** Pseudotumor cerebri, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, and hyperglycemia.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 45-year-old male with acromegaly and a persistent pituitary adenoma requires medical therapy. Name the long-acting somatostatin analog used and its most common gastrointestinal side effect.
back:
Octreotide (or Lanreotide)
*   **Clinical Uses:** Acromegaly, carcinoid syndrome, VIPoma.
*   **Adverse Effects:** Biliary sludge/gallstones (due to inhibited gallbladder contraction) and steatorrhea.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Explain the pharmacological mechanism of continuous (non-pulsatile) Leuprolide administration in treating prostate cancer.
back:
Initial surge of LH/FSH followed by downregulation of pituitary GnRH receptors.
*   **Result:** Suppresses testosterone to castrate levels.
*   **Adverse Effects:** Hot flushes, reduced bone density, and initial 'tumor flare'.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Contrast the effects of Tamoxifen and Raloxifene on the risk of endometrial carcinoma.
back:
Tamoxifen: Agonist at endometrium; increases cancer risk.
*   Raloxifene: Antagonist at endometrium; no increased risk.
*   **Both:** Agonists in bone (prevent osteoporosis) and antagonists in breast (treat/prevent cancer).

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Specify the role and primary adverse effect of Bromocriptine in women with the amenorrhea-galactorrhea syndrome.
back:
D2 Dopamine Receptor Agonist; inhibits prolactin release.
*   **Clinical Uses:** Prolactinoma, Parkinson's disease.
*   **Adverse Effects:** Nausea, headache, and orthostatic hypotension.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: In patients with mild Hemophilia A or von Willebrand disease, the drug used to increase factor VIII levels is [___].
back:
Desmopressin (DDAVP)
*   **Mechanism:** Selective V2 receptor agonist.
*   **Adverse Effects:** Water intoxication/hyponatremia and headache.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A female patient undergoing ovulation induction presents with sudden weight gain, massive ovarian enlargement, and ascites. Name the causative drug class and the condition.
back:
Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS) caused by Gonadotropins (FSH/hCG).
*   **Clinical Use:** Infertility.
*   **Adverse Effects:** Multiple pregnancies and thromboembolism.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Describe why Finasteride is preferred over Flutamide for treating Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) regarding sexual function.
back:
Finasteride inhibits 5-alpha reductase (DHT reduction only), sparing systemic testosterone levels.
*   **Flutamide:** Competitive AR antagonist; causes significant impotence and gynecomastia.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Contrast the mechanism of Clomiphene with Mifepristone.
back:
Clomiphene: Partial ER agonist; blocks pituitary feedback to increase FSH/LH (ovulation induction).
*   Mifepristone: Progesterone/Glucocorticoid antagonist; used as an abortifacient (with misoprostol).

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Enumerate the most serious hepatic and physical adverse effects of chronic anabolic steroid (e.g., Oxandrolone) abuse in athletes.
back:
Hepatic: Cholestatic jaundice and hepatocellular carcinoma.
*   Physical: Testicular atrophy, azoospermia, and virilization in females.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Children with growth failure due to Turner syndrome or Prader-Willi syndrome are often treated with the recombinant human growth hormone known as [___].
back:
Somatropin.
- Clinical Uses: GH deficiency, Turner syndrome, Prader-Willi, and AIDS wasting.
- Adverse Effects: Pseudotumor cerebri, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, edema, and hyperglycemia.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 28-year-old female presents with galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and infertility. MRI shows a pituitary microadenoma. The pharmacological agent of choice acts on [___] receptors.
back:
Dopamine D2 receptors (Bromocriptine/Cabergoline).
- Clinical Uses: Hyperprolactinemia, acromegaly, and Parkinson's disease.
- Adverse Effects: Nausea, orthostatic hypotension, and psychiatric disturbances.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
coreConcept: GnRH Agonist Mechanism and Biphasic Effect
front: Explain the mechanism by which continuous administration of Leuprolide eventually suppresses gonadotropin secretion.
back:
- Mechanism: Downregulates GnRH receptors in the pituitary.
- Clinical Uses: Prostate cancer, endometriosis, and precocious puberty.
- Key Note: Initially causes a 'flare' (hormone surge) before suppression occurs.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Contrast the tissue-specific effects of Tamoxifen and Raloxifene on the endometrial lining.
back:
- Tamoxifen: Estrogen agonist in endometrium; increases risk of endometrial hyperplasia/cancer.
- Raloxifene: Estrogen antagonist in endometrium; no increased cancer risk.
- Both: Bone agonists (prevent osteoporosis) and breast antagonists.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Identify the primary clinical uses and the most dangerous electrolyte abnormality associated with Desmopressin therapy.
back:
- Clinical Uses: Central diabetes insipidus, Hemophilia A, and von Willebrand disease.
- Toxicity: Hyponatremia (water intoxication).
- Mechanism: Selective V2 receptor agonist increasing water reabsorption.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: To treat benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) while minimizing sexual side effects, the drug [___] is used to inhibit the production of dihydrotestosterone (DHT).
back:
Finasteride (5-alpha reductase inhibitor).
- Clinical Uses: BPH and male-pattern baldness.
- Adverse Effects: Decreased libido and gynecomastia (rare compared to receptor blockers).

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman on unopposed estrogen replacement therapy for hot flushes is at a significantly increased risk for which malignancy?
back:
Endometrial Carcinoma.
- Management: Must add a progestin (e.g., Medroxyprogesterone) to negate the hyperplastic effect.
- Other Risks: Thromboembolism, gallbladder disease, and migraine.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Describe the physiological bypass mechanism and the most critical acute toxicity of Mecasermin.
back:
- Mechanism: Recombinant IGF-1; bypasses defective GH receptors to promote growth.
- Clinical Use: GH-insensitive growth failure (Laron dwarfism).
- Critical Toxicity: Hypoglycemia (must be administered with food).

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Distinguish between the therapeutic onset of GnRH agonists (Leuprolide) and GnRH antagonists (Ganirelix) in ovulation induction.
back:
- Leuprolide: Delayed onset (~1 week); requires down-regulation after an initial flare.
- Ganirelix: Immediate onset; suppresses LH/FSH secretion without an initial surge.
- Use: Prevents premature LH surges.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Specify the pharmacological target and clinical indications for Mifepristone.
back:
- Target: Progesterone and glucocorticoid receptor antagonist.
- Clinical Uses: Medical abortion (with misoprostol) and postcoital contraception.
- Adverse Effects: Heavy vaginal bleeding and abdominal cramping.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: The recombinant form of human growth hormone used to treat Turner syndrome and Prader-Willi syndrome is [___].
back:
Somatropin.

*   **Uses:** GH deficiency, Turner syndrome, and AIDS wasting.
*   **Adverse Effects:** Pseudotumor cerebri, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, and hyperglycemia.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 27-year-old female presents with galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and infertility. MRI shows a pituitary microadenoma. The pharmacological treatment targets [___] receptors.
back:
Dopamine D2 receptors.

*   **Drug:** Bromocriptine or Cabergoline.
*   **Mechanism:** Inhibits prolactin release from pituitary lactotrophs.
*   **Adverse Effects:** Nausea, headache, and orthostatic hypotension.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Explain why continuous administration of Leuprolide is effective in treating advanced prostate cancer despite being a GnRH agonist.
back:
*   **Downregulation:** Continuous dosing desensitizes pituitary GnRH receptors.
*   **Outcome:** Suppression of FSH/LH release leads to castrate levels of testosterone.
*   **Note:** Initial 'flare' must be blocked with Flutamide.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: In a postmenopausal woman with a high risk of breast cancer and a history of endometrial hyperplasia, contrast the suitability of Tamoxifen versus Raloxifene.
back:
*   **Raloxifene:** Preferred; acts as an antagonist in both breast and endometrium.
*   **Tamoxifen:** Avoided; acts as an agonist in the endometrium, increasing cancer risk.
*   **Both:** Agonists in bone (prevent osteoporosis).

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Identify the clinical advantage of using Finasteride over Flutamide in the management of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH).
back:
*   **Finasteride:** Inhibits 5-alpha-reductase, selectively lowering DHT.
*   **Benefit:** Spares systemic testosterone, causing less impotence and loss of libido than the receptor blocker Flutamide.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: The selective V2 receptor agonist used to treat Central Diabetes Insipidus and Mild Hemophilia A is [___].
back:
Desmopressin (dDAVP).

*   **Uses:** Central DI, Nocturnal enuresis, and von Willebrand disease.
*   **Adverse Effects:** Water intoxication and hyponatremia.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A woman undergoing IVF treatment with Follitropin and hCG suddenly develops abdominal pain, ascites, and hypovolemia. Identify the likely complication.
back:
Ovarian Hyperstimulation Syndrome (OHSS).

*   **Cause:** Excessive ovarian response to gonadotropins.
*   **Clinical Signs:** Ovarian enlargement, pleural effusion, and potential shock.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Describe the mechanism by which Mifepristone acts as an abortifacient and identify the adjuvant drug required for complete abortion.
back:
*   **Mechanism:** Competitive antagonist at Progesterone and Glucocorticoid receptors, causing luteolysis.
*   **Adjuvant:** Misoprostol (PGE1 analog) to stimulate uterine contractions.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Distinguish between the clinical applications of Anastrozole and Danazol in female endocrine disorders.
back:
*   **Anastrozole:** Aromatase inhibitor used for estrogen-dependent breast cancer in postmenopausal women.
*   **Danazol:** Partial androgen agonist used for endometriosis; causes hirsutism and weight gain.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Enumerate the primary clinical indications for intravenous Oxytocin and its most dangerous maternal adverse effect.
back:
*   **Indications:** Labor induction, augmentation of weak contractions, and postpartum hemorrhage control.
*   **Adverse Effects:** Uterine rupture, water intoxication (due to ADH-like effect), and fetal distress.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: The recombinant human growth hormone used to treat growth failure in children with Turner syndrome or Prader-Willi syndrome is [___].
back:
• Somatropin.
• Clinical Uses: GH deficiency, AIDS wasting, short bowel syndrome.
• Adverse Effects: Pseudotumor cerebri, slipped capital femoral epiphysis, peripheral edema, and hyperglycemia.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 28-year-old female presents with galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and infertility. MRI reveals a pituitary microadenoma. Identify the first-line pharmacological treatment and its common side effects.
back:
• Bromocriptine or Cabergoline (Dopamine D2 agonists).
• Clinical Uses: Hyperprolactinemia, acromegaly, Parkinson's disease.
• Adverse Effects: Nausea, headache, orthostatic hypotension, and psychiatric disturbances.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Explain the physiological mechanism by which continuous administration of Leuprolide treats advanced prostate cancer.
back:
• Mechanism: Continuous GnRH receptor stimulation leads to receptor downregulation and pituitary desensitization.
• Result: Profound decrease in LH and testosterone secretion.
• Clinical Uses: Prostate cancer, endometriosis, precocious puberty.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Contrast the effects of Tamoxifen and Raloxifene on the endometrium and their clinical implications for postmenopausal women.
back:
• Tamoxifen: Estrogen agonist on endometrium (increases hyperplasia/cancer risk).
• Raloxifene: Estrogen antagonist on endometrium (safer for uterine tissue).
• Both: Agonists in bone (prevent osteoporosis), antagonists in breast (treat/prevent cancer).

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Describe the specific enzymatic target of Finasteride and its clinical utility in elderly males.
back:
• Target: Inhibits 5-alpha reductase (blocks conversion of Testosterone to Dihydrotestosterone).
• Clinical Uses: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) and male-pattern baldness.
• Adverse Effects: Rarely causes impotence or gynecomastia.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A synthetic 14-amino-acid peptide analog used to treat acromegaly and secretory diarrhea associated with carcinoid tumors is [___].
back:
• Octreotide.
• Mechanism: Somatostatin receptor agonist.
• Adverse Effects: Biliary sludge, gallstones (cholelithiasis), nausea, and cardiac conduction abnormalities.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A woman using combined oral contraceptives is prescribed Rifampin for tuberculosis. Predict the clinical outcome and explain the pharmacological basis.
back:
• Outcome: Increased risk of unintended pregnancy.
• Mechanism: Rifampin induces Cytochrome P450 (CYP3A4), accelerating the metabolism of estrogen and progestin.
• Adverse Effect: Breakthrough bleeding or contraceptive failure.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Identify the drug used for medical abortion within 49 days of gestation and explain its combined regimen for efficacy.
back:
• Mifepristone (Progesterone antagonist).
• Regimen: Combined with Misoprostol (PGE1 analog) to trigger uterine contractions.
• Adverse Effects: Heavy vaginal bleeding, GI distress, and risk of rare serious infections.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Distinguish between GnRH agonists (e.g., Leuprolide) and GnRH antagonists (e.g., Degarelix) regarding the 'flare effect' in prostate cancer treatment.
back:
• Agonists: Cause transient LH/testosterone surge ('flare') before downregulation; requires concurrent Flutamide initially.
• Antagonists: Provide immediate testosterone suppression without a flare.
• Use: Both treat advanced prostate carcinoma.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: List the primary clinical uses of Oxytocin and its most significant life-threatening adverse effect during over-administration.
back:
• Clinical Uses: Induction/augmentation of labor, control of postpartum hemorrhage.
• Adverse Effects: Uterine rupture, fetal distress, and water intoxication/hyponatremia (due to ADH-like effect).

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: In the treatment of children with growth failure due to Turner syndrome or Prader-Willi syndrome, the recombinant form of human GH used is [___].
back: Somatropin. Key clinical uses include GH deficiency, short bowel syndrome, and HIV-associated wasting.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A 27-year-old female presents with galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and infertility. Investigations confirm a prolactinoma. Identify the first-line pharmacological treatment and its most common adverse effects.
back: Bromocriptine (D2 agonist). Adverse effects include nausea, headache, orthostatic hypotension, and occasionally psychiatric disturbances.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Explain the tissue-specific mechanism of Tamoxifen that distinguishes its use in breast cancer from its risk in the uterus.
back: Tamoxifen acts as an estrogen receptor antagonist in breast tissue (inhibiting tumor growth) but as a partial agonist in the endometrium (increasing risk of endometrial cancer).

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Contrast the immediate hormonal response of Ganirelix with the initial response of Leuprolide when used for controlled ovarian hyperstimulation.
back: Ganirelix (Antagonist) provides immediate suppression of gonadotropins. Leuprolide (Agonist) causes an initial 'flare' (LH/FSH surge) before eventual receptor downregulation and suppression.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: Enumerate the primary clinical uses and two major gastrointestinal adverse effects of Octreotide.
back: Uses: Acromegaly, carcinoid syndrome, and acute variceal bleeding. Adverse effects: Gallstones (cholelithiasis) and steatorrhea/GI disturbances.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: The primary drug used to treat benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) by inhibiting the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone is [___].
back: Finasteride. It is a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor also used for male-pattern baldness.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
front: A patient with pituitary diabetes insipidus is started on Desmopressin. Beyond polyuria, identify another clinical indication and a critical electrolyte imbalance to monitor.
back: Indications: Hemophilia A or von Willebrand disease. Monitor for: Hyponatremia due to excessive water retention.

category: Enumerate their clinical uses and potential adverse effects
